title: A Schedulability Compatible Multiprocessor Resource Sharing Protocol -- MrsP

extraction.paper_name: A Schedulability Compatible Multiprocessor Resource Sharing Protocol -MrsP
extraction.paper_description: This paper proposes MrsP, a multiprocessor resource sharing protocol for partitioned fixed-priority systems. It extends the single-processor Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP/SRP) by introducing a 'helping' mechanism where busy-waiting tasks can execute critical sections on behalf of preempted tasks. The main contribution is a schedulability analysis framework that allows the application of single-processor response-time analysis, with adjusted resource access costs to account for multiprocessor contention and the helping mechanism.

variables.e_j: execution time parameter of resource r_j
variables.map: function mapping a set of tasks to the set of processors they are allocated to
variables.G_r_j: set of tasks that use resource r_j
variables.c_j: worst-case execution time of resource r_j

assumptions: r_j is a resource.
G_r_j is the set of tasks using r_j.
map(task_set) returns the set of processors onto which the tasks in task_set have been allocated.
abs(set) denotes the size of the set.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the total execution time cost for resource r_j, reflecting the number of potential parallel accesses from different processors.

informal_sketch.intuition: When a resource is shared across multiple processors, the total 'cost' of using it isn't just the critical section time (c_j), but also includes the time spent waiting for other processors to finish their access. This definition calculates that total cost by multiplying the critical section time by the number of distinct processors that can access the resource.
steps: Identify the resource r_j.
Determine the set of tasks G_r_j that use r_j.
Find the set of processors map(G_r_j) on which these tasks are allocated.
Count the number of unique processors in map(G_r_j) (abs(map(G_r_j))).
Multiply this count by the resource's individual critical section execution time c_j to get e_j.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_resource_execution_cost(resource_j, task_to_processor_map_func, tasks_using_resource_j, critical_section_time_j):
    # G_r_j is tasks_using_resource_j
    # map(G_r_j) is the set of processors where these tasks are allocated
    processors_accessing_resource = set()
    for task in tasks_using_resource_j:
        # Assuming task_to_processor_map_func(task) returns the processor for a single task
        processors_accessing_resource.add(task_to_processor_map_func(task))
    
    num_processors_accessing = len(processors_accessing_resource)
    e_j = num_processors_accessing * critical_section_time_j
    return e_j
key_insights: The cost e_j scales with the number of processors involved, not just the number of tasks.
If a resource is only used by tasks on a single processor, e_j = c_j.

G_r_j is the set of tasks using r_j.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the ceiling priority of a resource on a single processor, which is the highest priority of any task that accesses it.

informal_sketch.intuition: To prevent priority inversion and deadlocks on a single processor, a resource is assigned a 'ceiling priority'. This ceiling is the highest priority among all tasks that might ever access that resource. When a task accesses the resource, its effective priority is temporarily raised to this ceiling.
steps: Identify the resource r_j.
List all tasks G_r_j that access r_j.
For each task in G_r_j, find its base priority Pri_tau_k.
The ceiling priority Pri_r_j is the maximum of these task priorities.
key_insights: The ceiling priority mechanism ensures that a task holding a resource cannot be preempted by another task that might also need that resource, thus preventing deadlocks and limiting blocking.

formal_description.statement: C_i = WCET_i + sum(n_i_j * c_j) for all r_j in F_tau_i

variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task tau_i
variables.WCET_i: worst-case execution time of task tau_i, ignoring time spent executing critical sections
variables.n_i_j: number of times task tau_i uses resource r_j
variables.c_j: worst-case execution time of resource r_j
variables.F_tau_i: set of resources used by task tau_i

assumptions: This definition applies to single processor systems (PCP/SRP context).
tau_i is a task.
r_j is a resource.
F_tau_i is the set of resources used by task tau_i.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the total worst-case execution time of task tau_i, including the cumulative time spent in its critical sections.

informal_sketch.intuition: A task's total execution time isn't just its own computation; it also includes all the time it spends inside critical sections accessing shared resources. This formula sums up these components.
steps: Start with the task's base computation time WCET_i (excluding resource access).
For each resource r_j that task tau_i uses (from F_tau_i):
Multiply the number of times tau_i accesses r_j (n_i_j) by the execution time of r_j (c_j).
Sum these products for all resources.
Add this sum to WCET_i to get the total C_i.
key_insights: This decomposition helps separate the task's inherent computation from its resource-related overheads, which can be affected by resource sharing protocols.

variables.c_hat: maximum computation time of all resources that are used by at least one task with priority less than that of tau_i and at least one task with an equal or higher priority
variables.b: maximum non-preemptive execution time induced by the RTOS

assumptions: This definition applies to single processor systems (PCP/SRP context).
tau_i is a task.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the maximum blocking time that task tau_i can experience due to lower priority tasks accessing resources or RTOS overheads.

informal_sketch.intuition: A higher priority task can be blocked by a lower priority task if the lower priority task holds a resource with a high ceiling priority, or if the RTOS itself has non-preemptive sections. This formula captures the worst-case of these blocking scenarios.
steps: Identify c_hat: the longest critical section of a resource that could cause priority inversion for tau_i (i.e., a resource used by both lower and higher/equal priority tasks).
Identify b: the longest non-preemptive section of the RTOS.
The blocking term B_i is the maximum of these two values.
key_insights: Blocking is a critical component of schedulability analysis, representing delays caused by lower priority entities.
PCP/SRP aims to minimize c_hat by ensuring blocking occurs at most once and before execution.

formal_description.statement: R_i = C_i + B_i + sum(ceil(R_i / T_j) * C_j) for all tau_j in hp_i

variables.R_i: worst-case response time of task tau_i
variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task tau_i (from Definition 5)
variables.B_i: blocking term for task tau_i (from Definition 4)
variables.C_j: worst-case execution time of task tau_j
variables.hp_i: set of tasks with priority greater than tau_i

assumptions: This definition applies to single processor fixed-priority systems (PCP/SRP context).
tau_i is a task.
ceil(x) is the ceiling function, returning the smallest integer greater than or equal to x.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the worst-case response time of task tau_i, which is the maximum time from its release until its completion, considering its own execution, blocking, and interference from higher priority tasks.

informal_sketch.intuition: A task's response time is the sum of its own execution, any blocking it experiences, and the interference from higher priority tasks that preempt it. This equation is the standard iterative formula for calculating response times in fixed-priority single-processor systems.
steps: Initialize R_i to C_i + B_i (a lower bound).
Iteratively refine R_i:

Calculate the interference from each higher priority task tau_j in hp_i: (ceil(R_i_current / T_j) * C_j). This represents the total execution time of tau_j's jobs that can preempt tau_i within R_i_current.
Sum this interference for all tau_j in hp_i.
Update R_i_next = C_i + B_i + sum_of_interference.
Repeat until R_i_next == R_i_current or R_i_next > D_i (indicating unschedulability).
If R_i_next <= D_i, then R_i is the worst-case response time.
key_insights: This is a fundamental equation in real-time schedulability analysis.
It's an iterative fixed-point calculation because interference depends on the response time itself.
Schedulability requires R_i <= D_i.

formal_description.statement: Pri_r_j_p_k = max(Pri_tau_i) for all tau_i where tau_i in G_r_j and map_tau_i = {p_k}

variables.Pri_r_j_p_k: ceiling priority of resource r_j on processor p_k
variables.G_r_j: set of tasks that use resource r_j
variables.map_tau_i: processor to which task tau_i is allocated (represented as a set containing one processor)

assumptions: This definition applies to MrsP in partitioned multiprocessor systems.
r_j is a resource.
p_k is a processor.
G_r_j is the set of tasks using r_j.
map(task) returns the set of processors to which a task is allocated (for partitioned systems, this is a singleton set).
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the local ceiling priority for resource r_j on a specific processor p_k, which is the highest priority of any task allocated to p_k that uses r_j.

informal_sketch.intuition: In a multiprocessor system, each processor can have its own 'local' ceiling for a shared resource. This local ceiling is determined by the highest priority task on that specific processor that accesses the resource. This allows for local PCP/SRP behavior on each processor.
steps: Identify the resource r_j and the processor p_k.
Filter the set of tasks G_r_j to include only those tasks that are allocated to processor p_k.
From this filtered set, find the task with the highest priority Pri_tau_i.
This highest priority is the local ceiling priority Pri_r_j_p_k.
key_insights: MrsP uses per-processor ceiling priorities to enable local PCP/SRP behavior.
This allows tasks to execute with a raised priority locally, preventing preemption by other local tasks that might need the same resource.

formal_description.statement: At most one task per processor can be attempting to access any specific resource.
assumptions: MrsP protocol rules 1-4 are followed:
1. All resources are assigned a set of ceiling priorities, one per processor (Definition 8).
2. An access request on any resource results in the priority of the task being immediately raised to the local ceiling for the resource.
3. Accesses to a resource are dealt with in a FIFO order.

4. While waiting to gain access to the resource, and while actually using the resource, the task continues to be active and executes (possible spinning) with priority equal to the local ceiling of the resource.
Properties of PCP/SRP are applicable locally.
formal_description.conclusion: Limits the number of concurrent attempts to access a resource from tasks on the same processor to one.

informal_sketch.intuition: Because MrsP implements a local PCP/SRP on each processor, once a task on a processor starts trying to access a resource (and raises its priority to the local ceiling), no other task on that *same* processor can preempt it and also try to access that *same* resource. Any other local task that might need the resource would have a priority lower than or equal to the resource's local ceiling, and thus would be blocked.
steps: A task tau_A on processor p_k requests resource r_j.
According to MrsP rule 2, tau_A's priority is raised to Pri_r_j_p_k (Definition 8).
According to MrsP rule 4, tau_A remains active and executes at this priority.
If another task tau_B on the same processor p_k also requests r_j, its priority would also be raised to Pri_r_j_p_k.

However, due to PCP/SRP properties, tau_B cannot preempt tau_A if tau_A is already at Pri_r_j_p_k and tau_B's priority is not strictly higher. Since Pri_r_j_p_k is the maximum priority of any task on p_k accessing r_j, no other task on p_k can have a strictly higher priority and also access r_j.
Therefore, only one task from p_k can be actively attempting to access r_j at any given time.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def check_lemma_1(processor_k, resource_j, active_tasks_on_processor, task_priorities, resource_local_ceilings):
    # This lemma describes a property of the protocol's runtime behavior.
    # It's a guarantee derived from the protocol rules and PCP/SRP properties.
    
    # Conceptually, if multiple tasks on processor_k attempt to access resource_j,
    # only one can actually execute at the resource's local ceiling priority at a time.
    # The others would be locally blocked.
    
    # The proof relies on the fact that a task's priority is raised to the local ceiling
    # when accessing a resource, and this ceiling is the highest priority of any task
    # on that processor that uses the resource. Thus, no other local task can preempt it
    # to access the same resource.
    return True # Lemma holds by protocol design
key_insights: Local priority ceiling emulation is key to this property.
It ensures that within a single processor, resource access attempts are serialized, even if the resource is globally shared.

formal_description.statement: The maximum length of the FIFO queue for resource r_k is abs(map(G_r_k)).

variables.map: function mapping a set of tasks to the set of processors they are allocated to
variables.G_r_k: set of tasks that use resource r_k

assumptions: MrsP protocol rules are followed.
Lemma 1 holds: At most one task per processor can be attempting to access any specific resource.
formal_description.conclusion: Bounds the maximum number of tasks that can be simultaneously waiting in the FIFO queue for a global resource.

informal_sketch.intuition: Since only one task from any given processor can attempt to access a resource at a time (Lemma 1), the maximum number of tasks waiting for a resource in a global FIFO queue is limited by the number of distinct processors that have tasks accessing that resource.
steps: Identify the resource r_k.
Determine the set of tasks G_r_k that use r_k.
Find the set of processors map(G_r_k) on which these tasks are allocated.
Count the number of unique processors in map(G_r_k).

This count directly corresponds to the maximum number of tasks that can be in the FIFO queue (including the one currently using the resource), because each processor can contribute at most one task to the queue at any time.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_max_fifo_queue_length(resource_k, tasks_using_resource_k, task_to_processor_map_func):
    # Based on Lemma 1, only one task per processor can be attempting to access the resource.
    # So, the queue length is limited by the number of unique processors involved.
    processors_involved = set()
    for task in tasks_using_resource_k:
        processors_involved.add(task_to_processor_map_func(task))
    
    max_queue_length = len(processors_involved)
    return max_queue_length
key_insights: This lemma is crucial for bounding the blocking time for global resources.
It leverages the local PCP/SRP behavior (Lemma 1) to limit global contention.

formal_description.statement: Each job can suffer at most a single local block, and this blocking will occur before it actually executes.
assumptions: MrsP protocol rules 1-4 are followed (as listed in Lemma 1).
MrsP behaves according to the properties of PCP/SRP locally.
formal_description.conclusion: Guarantees that a job, once it starts executing, will not be blocked by local lower-priority tasks accessing resources it needs, and any blocking it does experience happens at the very beginning of its execution.

informal_sketch.intuition: Similar to single-processor PCP/SRP, MrsP's local priority ceiling mechanism ensures that once a job is dispatched and starts executing, all resources it might need are 'logically' available. Any blocking it might suffer from a lower priority task (which holds a resource with a higher ceiling) must occur before the job itself begins its execution.
steps: A job of task tau_i is released.
It attempts to execute.
If a lower priority task on the same processor is currently holding a resource with a local ceiling priority higher than or equal to tau_i's base priority, tau_i will be blocked.
However, once tau_i starts executing (meaning no such blocking condition exists), its priority will be raised to the local ceiling of any resource it accesses (MrsP rule 2).

Due to PCP/SRP properties, no newly released local job can preempt tau_i and then access a resource that tau_i might need, because tau_i is already running at a sufficiently high priority (its own or a resource ceiling).
Therefore, any blocking is confined to the initial dispatch phase.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def check_lemma_3(job, processor_state, resource_locks, task_priorities, resource_local_ceilings):
    # This lemma describes a property of the protocol's runtime behavior.
    # It's a guarantee derived from the protocol rules and PCP/SRP properties.
    
    # The proof relies on the local PCP/SRP behavior: a job can only start executing
    # if its priority is the highest and its preemption level is greater than the system ceiling.
    # Once it starts, all resources it needs are logically available, preventing further local blocking.
    return True # Lemma holds by protocol design
key_insights: This property simplifies schedulability analysis by limiting the complexity of blocking scenarios.
It's a direct carry-over of a key benefit from single-processor PCP/SRP to the local behavior of MrsP.

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the worst-case response time of task tau_i under MrsP, considering its own execution (with adjusted resource costs), blocking from local lower-priority tasks, and interference from local higher-priority tasks.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the core response-time analysis equation for MrsP. It's structurally identical to the single-processor RTA (Definition 3), but it uses MrsP-specific values for task execution time (C_i from Definition 7) and blocking (max(e_hat, b)). The interference term only considers *local* higher-priority tasks because of partitioning.
steps: Initialize R_i to C_i + max(e_hat, b).
Iteratively refine R_i:
Calculate the interference from each local higher priority task tau_j in hpl_i: (ceil(R_i_current / T_j) * C_j).
Sum this interference for all tau_j in hpl_i.
Update R_i_next = C_i + max(e_hat, b) + sum_of_interference.
Repeat until R_i_next == R_i_current or R_i_next > D_i.
If R_i_next <= D_i, then R_i is the worst-case response time.
key_insights: The structure of the RTA remains the same as single-processor, simplifying analysis.
The key changes are the definition of C_i (using e_j) and the blocking term (using e_hat), and considering only local interference.
This equation is the basis for proving MrsP's schedulability.

formal_description.statement: The worst-case response time of a task executing under MrsP is given by equations (4) and (5).

variables.R_i: worst-case response time of task tau_i (from Definition 6)
variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task tau_i (from Definition 7)

assumptions: MrsP protocol rules 1-6 are followed:
1. Resources assigned local ceiling priorities (Definition 8).
2. Task priority raised to local ceiling on resource access.
3. Resource accesses are FIFO.
4. Task executes at local ceiling priority while waiting/using resource.
5. Any task waiting for a resource can undertake computation for other waiting tasks (helping).
6. Cooperating task undertakes outstanding requests in FIFO order.
Lemma 3 holds: Each job suffers at most a single local block, occurring before execution.
formal_description.conclusion: Equations (4) and (5) (Definitions 6 and 7) provide a correct and safe upper bound for the worst-case response time of tasks under MrsP.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem validates that the proposed MrsP protocol, with its 'helping' mechanism, allows us to use a familiar single-processor RTA structure for multiprocessor systems. The key is that the helping mechanism ensures that even if a task is preempted while holding a resource, the work on that resource still progresses, effectively bounding the resource access time to e_j.
steps: **For C_i (Equation 5 / Definition 7):**
Consider a task tau_i accessing a resource r_j. In the worst case, tau_i will have to 'help' complete the critical sections for all other tasks that are ahead of it in the FIFO queue for r_j.
The maximum length of this queue is determined by the number of processors accessing r_j (Lemma 2).

The 'helping' mechanism (MrsP rules 5 & 6) ensures that even if tau_i is locally preempted while waiting or holding the resource, the work for r_j (including its own and others' turns) will still be completed by *some* task, effectively costing e_j.
Therefore, the sum of n_i_j * e_j accurately captures the worst-case time tau_i spends on resource accesses.
**For R_i (Equation 4 / Definition 6):**
The blocking term max(e_hat, b) captures the maximum time a lower priority task can execute with an inherited ceiling priority equal to or higher than tau_i's priority, or RTOS overhead.
Lemma 3 guarantees that this blocking occurs at most once and before tau_i's execution, consistent with the RTA model.
The interference term sum(ceil(R_i / T_j) * C_j) for local higher priority tasks is standard for partitioned fixed-priority systems.
Combining these components, the RTA equation (4) correctly calculates the worst-case response time.

This theorem bridges the gap between the protocol's operational rules and its analytical schedulability model.
It demonstrates that MrsP achieves its goal of being 'schedulability compatible' with single-processor RTA.

variables.e_i: execution time parameter for potentially nested resource r_i
variables.V_r_i: set of resources that access r_i (i.e., r_i is nested within them)
variables.map: function mapping a set of tasks to the set of processors they are allocated to
variables.G_r_i: set of tasks that directly use resource r_i
variables.c_i: worst-case execution time of resource r_i

assumptions: This definition applies to MrsP with nested resource usage.
r_i is a resource.
V_r_i is the set of resources that access r_i.
G_r_i is the set of tasks that directly use r_i.
Ordered locking is assumed for deadlock prevention (though not formally covered in this paper).
formal_description.conclusion: Extends the definition of resource execution cost (e_j) to account for nested resource accesses, where the queue length is influenced by both direct callers and callers via other resources.

informal_sketch.intuition: When resources are nested (e.g., r_a calls r_b), the queue for the inner resource (r_b) can be longer than just the number of processors directly accessing r_b. It also includes tasks that are accessing r_b indirectly through r_a. This formula accounts for both direct and indirect callers to determine the worst-case queue length and thus the total execution cost.
steps: Identify the resource r_i.

Determine the set of resources V_r_i that access r_i (i.e., r_i is an inner resource for them). The size abs(V_r_i) represents the maximum number of tasks that could be waiting for r_i due to nested calls from other resources.

Determine the set of processors map(G_r_i) that have tasks directly accessing r_i. The size abs(map(G_r_i)) represents the maximum number of tasks that could be waiting for r_i due to direct calls (by Lemma 2).
Sum these two counts: abs(V_r_i) + abs(map(G_r_i)). This is the maximum effective queue length for r_i.
Multiply this total queue length by the resource's individual critical section execution time c_i to get e_i.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_nested_resource_execution_cost(resource_i, resources_accessing_resource_i, tasks_directly_using_resource_i, task_to_processor_map_func, critical_section_time_i):
    # Max tasks waiting from nested calls (one per outer resource, as outer resource serializes)
    num_nested_callers = len(resources_accessing_resource_i)
    
    # Max tasks waiting from direct calls (one per processor, by Lemma 2)
    processors_direct_accessing = set()
    for task in tasks_directly_using_resource_i:
        processors_direct_accessing.add(task_to_processor_map_func(task))
    num_direct_callers = len(processors_direct_accessing)
    
    total_effective_queue_length = num_nested_callers + num_direct_callers
    e_i = total_effective_queue_length * critical_section_time_i
    return e_i
key_insights: Nested resource usage complicates queue length calculation.
The formula accounts for the serialization imposed by outer resources, ensuring that only one task from a given outer resource can be waiting for an inner resource.
This extended e_i would then be used in Definition 7 for tasks accessing nested resources.
